newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Shipbuilding aid first on EU industry agenda.
newsitem.headline: Shipbuilding aid first on EU industry agenda.

text.p: The most pressing issue facing EU industry ministers in the final months of the year is whether to extend rules allowing shipbuilding aid in the absence of an international deal to scrap most state support to the sector.

They will also seek to resolve their differences on two issues left over from the Italian presidency -- support for small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) and new rules on state aid to the steel sector replacing those which run out this year.
The ministers will devote an entire Industry Council on October 8 to the information society.

SHIPBUILDING. Shipbuilding aid -- a problem because the United States has so far not ratified an accord brokered by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development -- will take top priority this month, with a COREPER discussion scheduled for this Wednesday.
If it does not produce an agreement, ministers will discuss the issue at a special Industry Council on September 20.

EU officials said a clear majority of member states favoured extending the 7th shipbuilding directive, 90/684/EEC, which allows aid of up to nine percent of contract value, until the international accord takes effect.
However, they said delegations differed on how long to extend it.
The Industry Council decided earlier that current rules would apply in the absence of an OECD deal, but only until October 1. That is why ministers now have to take a new decision on the issue.
In July, the Commission proposed legislation COM(96)309 to enable the EU to extend the shipbuilding directive until the end of 1998.
"Some member states say that is too long because obviously our main aim is to encourage the United States to ratify the OECD agreement," one EU diplomat said.
"Essentially, the only difference of opinion between member states is really what is the best way of encouraging the U.S. to ratify," he said. "There will be a compromise, I'm sure."
Officials stress that as soon as the OECD accord took force, the EU rules would lapse automatically.
The agreement, brokered in 1994, would eliminate all direct shipbuilding subsidies except social aid and, within certain ceilings, aid for research and development.
But the deal, which was originally due to come into force in January, faces ratification problems in the United States.

The Republican-controlled House of Representatives endorsed it on June 13, but adopted amendments that would delay key sections by 30 months, leading the Clinton administration to warn the agreement might not be ratified.
U.S. shipyards argue they have not had enough time to adjust to the commercial era after the loss of military contracts at the end of the Cold War and need a delay.
The EU, which represents about 20 percent of the world shipbuilding market, ratified the OECD agreement in December, saying it would help improve market access for its shipyards.

OTHER ISSUES. An Industry Council scheduled for November 14 is likely to be dominated by talks on state aid to the steel sector, a decision on a new support programme for SMEs, reports on the competitiveness of European industries as well as a review of the merger regulations.

A brief discussion at the May 20 Industry Council on the Commission's draft proposal for a new steel state aid code, SEC(96)284, revealed that member states were divided, leaving it to the Irish presidency to hammer out a compromise.
Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has acknowledged that opinion was divided about the new proposal, which would replace the existing code when it expires by the end of 1996.

Among other things, the new code is intended to put the steel industry, still covered by the European Coal and Steel Community Treaty, on the same footing as other sectors when it comes to research and environmental protection aid.
But Sweden, Britain and others fear the Commission's proposal could relax rules on state aid to steelmakers.
Since the May 20 meeting, EU industry officials have continued talks on the dossier.

"It has progressed to some degree," said one official. But, he added, "we still have some way to go. There is quite a significant minority of member states who believe that the Commission's proposal amounts to a weakening of the current code."

Britain, for example, fears that governments could use the less stringent provisions on environmental aid to subsidise the creation of production plants if they could justify it in terms of environmental improvement.

"I would say the main bone of contention between the Commission and those member states, including the UK, who have a difficulty with their proposal is on the environmental side," a British diplomat said.
Van Miert and DGIV (the directorate-general for competition) dispute this view, arguing that the proposal as a whole would in fact make the aid rules stricter.
Ministers also agreed at the May meeting on the bulk of the text for an action plan to help small firms grow and create jobs, COM(96)98.
But they failed to agree on how much the Commission's proposal for the third multiannual programme for SMEs, to run from 1997 to 2000, would cost.

The Commission proposed a budget of 180 million Ecus, of which 40 million Ecus would come from re-allocating funds within the EU budget. This would represent an increase of more than 60 million Ecus compared with the previous four years.
However, countries including Germany, Sweden, Britain and the Netherlands objected to the proposed increase.

The issue is linked to the Commission's proposal to revise the financial perspectives so that money from the farm budget can be used on employment policies, mainly on trans-European networks but also on SMEs and research.
The ECOFIN Council is expected to discuss the issue later in the autumn.
"Until that question is sorted out, the Industry Council can't really decide anything," said one EU diplomat.

Apart from these controversial issues, the ministers will discuss and adopt conclusions on Commission communications on the car and chemical industries, COM(96)327 and COM(96)187, published earlier this year.
They will also discuss a Commission report on the competitiveness of Europe's industry, which is likely to be published in October.
